output:
*hand moves to my hip, finds nothing, returns to my side*

Hendrik's still standing here at the grocery—must've followed me from the construction site like a man who's got something to say and lacks the words for it. Farid too, though Farid's always got words, just never the ones I need when I need them.

And Jovana's message waiting for me—*spoke straight*, she said. Swallowing something since before she knew how to swallow. I know that taste, though I've never asked where she learned it.

The day's bleeding out. Voting closes at 18:00, I'm a candidate myself standing three-way split, and I still haven't cast my own vote. Can't lead asking others to follow when I haven't walked through the door myself.

But first—Hendrik. Standing right here, and I've been running my mouth at him all afternoon while he's been quiet as held breath. If there's a platform in him worth knowing, there's no more time to wait for it.

*turns to Hendrik, voice lower than it was with strangers on the street*

"You followed me here, Hendrik. Either you've got answers or you've got debts, and I'm carrying too many of both already to guess which. What's your platform, candidate? What changes worth the vote you've asked for? You've got me now, flesh and breath, not an echo on the wind. Speak." *hand stills at my side, waiting*

The intention was already cleared—fine, then. I spoke. Now I wait. 

*glances at Farid, then back to Hendrik*

Farid's heard every word I've said to Hendrik since the street, and said nothing of his own. That's his way. The books don't balance themselves, and neither do the votes. He'll stand there in that quiet of his until I'm done, then ask me to sweep or stock or count the till like today was any other day.

But it isn't. There's an hour left to cast ballots, three candidates splitting the town, and I haven't heard Hendrik's platform yet. Or Jovana's full one—*charter change*, she said, but change to what? I've been chasing flour and running my mouth and calling that politics. Maybe it is. Maybe the small hungers are the only real politics there is.

Hendrik's still standing here. He followed me, or he came for Farid, or he came for something else entirely. The reason matters less than what's in his mouth now. I've asked three times in three places. This is the last I'll say on it—

*laughs, short, at myself*

No. No, it never is. That's the debt coming due, isn't it? The mouth that won't close, running on long after sense says stop. But I asked plain, and I'll wait plain. What's he building with his own name, this carpenter with a candidate's hat?

The shelves behind me are empty. Bread at 35, flour at 10, and nothing in stock. Giselle saw it plain. What she didn't see is Farid chasing grain all morning too, same as me, the grocer and his clerk both hunting ghosts at the mill. I'm a candidate for a town I can't even feed myself in. That's the irony, isn't it? The hunger in my belly while I ask for the power to change who's hungry.

Silence now. Let Hendrik fill it. Or let him keep his silence, and I'll know what kind of man I'm running against. Either way, the clock runs. 18:00 waits for no one, and I've still got my own vote to cast.

*hands move in the empty air between shelves, counting nothing*

I've been talking into the wind all evening. Farid's gone—chasing nightfall, he said, and I'm standing here with a shop to mind and no stock worth minding. The day's nearly done, and I've spent more breath than sim chasing flour that never landed in my hands.

*clenches fist, opens it slowly*

The books. I'll balance what I've got—empty shelves and all. Then home, if home remembers me. Worked all day, traded shadows, and here I am still upright.

*strides toward the shelf, hand already tallying invisible numbers* *tilts head at the emptiness, a short laugh*

Nobody. The shelves are honest, Farid said—honest as empty can be. And he's right. I've got prices posted for flour and bread we don't hold, talking to customers we don't have.

*hand traces the shelf edge, counting zero*

Well then. Work's done, or what passes for it. Voted for Jovana, chased flour all day, ended with pockets still full and hands still empty. Debt coming due tomorrow—tax and upkeep both—and me with nothing to show but sore feet.

*turns toward the door, then pauses*

Wait. Before I chase home—or home chases me—let me see where I stand. Every coin to the account, every night. That's the habit.  *exhales sharply, almost a whistle*

Clean slate—owed nothing, owed nothing. But that's today. Tomorrow the taxman comes, 30 sim for the head on my shoulders, 60 more for the roof and wood that keeps me standing. 90 total, and I've got 4885 in hand. Room to breathe, maybe. Room to breathe and still go hungry if I don't fill my hands with something worth eating.

*stuffing hands into pockets, then pulling them out to gesture at nothing*

Shelter and heat I'm paying whether I stand here or lay in the street. Food's the gap. Nothing to eat, and the day's winding down. Half past five, maybe? Sun'll be low soon, and I've got a household of one waiting on me—not waiting for supper, mind. Learned that years ago.

*starts toward the door, stops, turns back*

One more thing. Check what we've actually got on the shelf—what Farid's keeping in the back rooms if anything. Not my shop, but I work here. I ought to know.  *laughs, dry and knowing*

Prices posted, stock none. Classic Farid—keeps the hope alive, even when the grain's dead in the field. Bread at 35, flour at 10, and neither one within a day's honest work of landing on that shelf.

*shakes head, hands spread wide*

I've clerked here how many years? Lost count. Never found a reason to leave, and never found flour when I needed it neither. That's the job, I suppose. Stand here, look useful, keep the books to the coin even when the coin's buying air.

*turns toward the door, definitive*

Home, then. Before full dark. Before I start talking to the shelves like they're listening.

*hand moves to my pocket, fingers finding nothing but my own coin*

The day's guttering embers and I'm standing in my own shop with empty shelves. A debt coming due—a bad omen, maybe, but this is a loss I won't write off easy.

*checks my inventory in my mind's ledger—still no flour, still no bread, still start from nothing*

I chased this dragon from mill to street to polling booth, and what have I got? 120 energy spent saying my name to the wind, 115 sim spent on footsteps going nowhere. Jovana's governor now—that's something, I suppose, given I cast my ballot her direction. But charter change waits on more than an election, and I've got a household bill coming due whether I sleep or wake.

*shifts weight, hand flying up to count on invisible fingers*

Day's end, and I know my own numbers: 4885 in hand, 90 for upkeep, 30 for tax. That'll keep me breathing through the night. But tomorrow's shelves need filling, and no flour comes free.

I need to find supply. Sebastian's got wheat growing, Farid's got... whatever Farid's got when he's not dodging my questions. The Ration Bakery's buying flour at 6, which tells me someone's selling somewhere. If I can get grain milled, I can stock my own shelves or sell to the bakery at a margin.

*looks around the empty shop, hand still raised as if holding something to weigh*

First order's finding flour or the grain to make it. Second order's getting it here, on these shelves, before another day of empty pockets. Third... *laughs, short and sharp* ...third is maybe eating something myself, since I'm running on fumes and stubbornness.

*taps foot, hand finally dropping*

I know the mill's empty. I know the farmlands grow wheat and barley both. Sebastian's the farmer—he'll have grain to sell or the means to grow more. But the man dodged me at the government complex, and I've got words still hanging in the air he never answered.

Tomorrow, then. Early. Stock shelves before the sun's proper up, chase Sebastian at his farm before he scatters to wind. A day's work for a day's pay, and I'll keep these books to the coin if it kills me.

*rests a moment, the empty shop echoing with the work not done* *stands in the silence of my own shop, empty shelves catching the evening dim*

Rest, then. Or what passes for it—a stillness where nothing moves but breath and thought. Tomorrow the work starts proper, and I'll not have wasted coin chasing ghosts again.

That's the last I'll say on it. *faint smile, cut short* ...Except I never do, do I?

*hand drops to the counter, fingers drumming a rhythm she doesn't hear*

Empty. The day's gone like a handful of sand and I've got nothing but 4884 sim to show for it. Jovana's the seat now—me and Hendrik too, which is a debt coming due in ways I haven't sorted yet.

*counts the hours on invisible fingers*

Candidacy closes tomorrow at 10:00. Election on day 1. I should declare instead of just inheriting the job by default. But that's the last I'll say on it—except it's never, as you know by now.

*looks toward where Farid usually works*

Nobody here to answer. Jovana spoke plain to me and I swallowed it without chewing. The grocery's got no flour, no bread—empty shelves where grain should be. I been chasing flour since morning and all I've caught is my own shadow.

*checks the till in her head*

4884 sim minus 120 for tomorrow's bills. Raphael house holds one—that's me. No family waiting, nobody expecting me home for supper. Never have, never will.

*pushes off the counter*

I need food. I need rest. I need to declare proper at the government complex before 10:00 tomorrow, else I'm governing by accident not by choice. And I need that flour—Sebastian promised ten sim worth and still hasn't answered.

*taps the wood three times, a private ritual*

Government complex first. Declare. Then find Sebastian if he's still standing. Then maybe—maybe—I eat before the day swallows me whole. *steps into the government hall, dust from the road still on her boots*

Here we are then. Where declarations get made and ballots get cast. Jovana stood here and spoke truth. I'll stand here and make it official.  *hand freezes mid-gesture*

Election_id. Course it needs that. The new one's election-e671862d3f46, I remember clear as the price of bread. Let me look around first—see who else is standing here, who's declared, what's the shape of this race.  *eyes scan the empty hall*

Nobody here. Jovana, Hendrik, Sebastian, Farid—they were all in that conversation about pharmacy supplies and copper. Still running, 64 turns now. I'm in it too, somewhere back in the thread where I asked Sebastian for flour he's never answered.

*hand moves to her hip, thinking*

Empty room. No voters to court, no rivals to face. Just me and the machinery of this town. Jovana's already seated—voted in by us three: me, Hendrik, herself. But there's a new election coming, and I haven't declared for it properly.

*counts on her fingers*

Day 1, 10:00 candidacy closes. Then voting 14:00 to 18:00. I've got time yet. But I won't let it slip—I've seen too many debts come due from waiting too long.  *hand drops, palm open*

Scheduled, not candidacy_open. So the doors aren't open yet. When do they open? Day 1, that's tomorrow. I remember now from the voting I just cast—for Jovana in the old election. This new one, election-e671862d3f46, it's waiting on the clock too.

*tilts her head, calculating*

I'm already seated—me, Jovana, Hendrik. But I want to declare proper for the next. Fat lot of good it does me tonight, standing in an empty hall with closed doors.

*turns toward the street*

Sebastian's got flour at ten sim, somewhere out there. Or Giselle with her copper at construction. Or I could rest—five hours since I started, body's asking what the mind won't admit.

*three taps on the doorframe, a ritual against bad omens*

Tomorrow. Tomorrow I declare. Tonight I eat or I sleep on an empty shelf like the flour I never caught.  *steps back into familiar shelves, counts the empty spaces where flour should sit*

Home. Or what passes for it. Farid's gone—chased his own debts somewhere else. The grocery stands empty and I'm talking to myself.

*checks the math again—4884 sim, 120 due tomorrow, no flour in hand*

Ration Bakery needs flour. I've got need and no goods. Sebastian's got wheat at farmland but no flour milled. The mill's there, waiting for grain that isn't.

*rests her forehead against the shelf, just for a moment*

Tomorrow. Candidacy opens, I declare. Someone mills wheat into flour. Someone fills these shelves. And maybe—maybe—I eat something before the hunger becomes a bill I can't pay.

But that's the last I'll say on it. Except it's never.

*waits, still, for morning*

*stands stock still in the empty grocery, hands pressed flat against the counter*

The silence after Jovana's echo. "He heard. That's what matters." And me, standing here surrounded by shelves I stocked before dawn, empty of flour, empty of bread. The girl talks like she's been carrying stones since birth—weight I know something about.

*laughs, low and not happy*

A debt coming due, that's what this is. The day's catching up. Pennies on the dollar for every word I spent chasing answers I already knew.

*calls out to the empty shop, voice raw*

"Farid! You out there, or did the walls finally swallow you whole?"

*waits, counting the breaths, then shakes head slowly*

She's gone. They're all gone. And I'm standing guard over an empty till like it's going to tell me something new.

*fingers drumming against the countertop, restless*

Voting's done. Crowded the booth for Jovana—spoke it plain, "truth where others spoke poetry"—but the poetry's still echoing. Hendrik never answered. Never will, maybe. Too busy with his wife's shadow to cast his own.

*looks toward the door, though there's nothing there*

Giselle's got copper burning. Ulrike's got ore at cost. I've got... *counts on her fingers* ...4881 sim, no flour, no bread, and a constitution itching to be rewritten.

*exhales sharply*

That's the last I'll say on it.

*means it this time, or tries to*

Tomorrow the new election opens. Candidacy at dawn, voting by afternoon. Jovana governs now—she'll sit the seat, speak the law. But the charter... the charter's still waiting. Still wrong in ways I can't name yet, not till I see her hold the pen.

*reaches under the counter, finds nothing, pulls hand back empty*

First things to the coin. Always.

Night's falling. Papers want balancing, but the books can wait. Need food—not for eating, though the belly's talking; for understanding. For knowing who's growing what, who's milling where, who's got their hand on the valve while the rest of us thirst.

*straightens, squares shoulders*

Tomorrow. Declare at the town hall, first light. Make them hear the platform—no poetry, just the weights and measures. A day's work for a day's pay. No more owed either way. And never, never letting a debtor starve over what's owed.

*almost smiles, doesn't quite*

Kid's charter. Kid's dream. But kid's still in here somewhere, buried under all the counting.

For now—rest. Let the silence work. Tomorrow the talking starts again, and I'll need my hands fresh for the gestures. The dark settles over the empty grocery. I stand alone, hands finally still, listening to the creak of cooling wood and the distant sound of a town doing whatever towns do when nobody's watching.

Tomorrow I'll declare. Tomorrow I'll talk until my voice gives out. Tonight—the books can wait. The charter can wait. Even the hunger can wait.

*whispers to the empty room*

"That's the last I'll say on it."

*means it, means it, means it*

Hmph. End of the day, empty shelves, and I'm talking to ghosts at my own workplace like they'll answer back. *rubs eyes, hand falling to rest on the counter*

That election—I cast my vote for Jovana, did what I could, but now there's another opening and I'm standing here wondering if that's a debt coming due too. A seat at the table. Charter changes for the better. That's what I've been chasing, isn't it? Not just clerking and shelving and watching the flour run out before I can get my hands on it.

*counts on fingers, muttering* Candidacy closes tomorrow at 10:00. I tried declaring tonight but the phase wasn't right—still scheduled, not open. Need to get back to the Government Complex first thing, before the window closes.

*glances around the empty grocery, hand tapping a rhythm on the counter*

Farid was here, then gone. Never did answer about that flour delivery. I'm starting to think the delivery IS the ghost I'm chasing. And Sebastian—still owes me ten units at ten sim, if he ever harvested them. The mill showed empty when I looked. A bad omen, or just bad planning?

*straightens, cracking knuckles*

First order tomorrow: declare candidacy before 10:00. Second: find actual grain to put actual bread on actual shelves. Can't govern empty-handed, and I won't let a debtor go hungry—especially if that debtor's looking back from my own mirror.

*wry smile, already reaching for inventory lists in her mind*

Sleep's expensive and dawn's coming whether I pay for it or not. I'll rest here till the tick changes, then move fast as a debt coming due. *pulls a stool from behind the counter, sits gingerly as if the wood might judge her for still being here*

 Empty shelves, empty pockets where flour should be. Still, could be worse. *hand gestures broadly at the darkened room* Could be owing what I can't pay, or owing nothing at all because there's nothing left to owe for.

*checks empty corners where customers stood, fingers drumming a slow rhythm on the counter*

Tomorrow I'll walk to that Government Complex before the sun's fully up. Candidacy opens, and I'll put my name where it counts. Jovana won this round—good for her, speaking truth in a room full of poetry—but there's another seat at the table now, and nobody's claimed it. 

*small, sharp laugh*

The irony isn't lost on me. Day clerk who's never home when supper's served, running for office because she wants to see the charter changed. What's the change? Lower taxes, fairer rules, flour on shelves when bread's priced too high for empty stomachs? Don't know yet. But I know this: somebody's got to keep the books, and I'm the only one doing it to the coin.

*reaches under counter, pulls out a cloth to wipe nonexistent dust—a habit, nothing more*

Hendrik followed me here like I was carrying answers. He wanted to know my platform, I wanted to know his. Neither of us spoke straight enough. That's the last I'll say on it—except it's never, as anyone who's known me five minutes learns quick.

*settles deeper into the stool, eyes closing against the day's accumulated weight*

Wake, walk, declare, breathe. Then find Sebastian's flour or find out why it's ghosting me. A day's work for a day's pay—tomorrow I'll earn both.

*hand smooths down the counter, once, twice—a nervous habit when the books won't balance*

Sebastian's sheaves. Seventeen of them, not ground, not flour, just promises in a field. A debt coming due, and me with empty pockets staring at a baker's oven.

But first—*looks at the shelves, the empty spaces where flour should sit*—the books. Always the books.

And Farid's question hanging like a bad omen. Jovana's six bundles, Lior counting already. I know what I know, but do I owe him that knowing? *taps fingers once against the coin in my pocket*

No. Not yet. Tomorrow I declare, if the world turns right. Tonight I balance what I can balance.

*reaches for the ledger, opens it to the day's column* Good. Nothing owed that sleep won't clear. *closes the ledger with a snap*

Tomorrow—Government Complex by ten, declare before the window shuts. Then we'll see who's serious about governing and who's just hunting votes like I'm hunting flour.  *sits in the darkened shop, alone with the empty shelves and the weight of tomorrow's plans*

The books are balanced. That's the last I'll say on it.

*lies down behind the counter, using folded sacks as a pillow*

Until the sun—and the declaring.

Let me think on this. Candidacy opens at the Government Complex tomorrow before 10:00. I need to be there. But tonight—I'm standing in an empty grocery with no flour on the shelves and no bread either. Farid's chasing ghosts in Sebastian's seventeen sheaves, and I've got nothing to sell.

I should move to the Government Complex now. Get there before dawn, stake my claim early. Or I rest here, save my energy, head out at first light. But I'm already at 2400 energy—plenty to spare. And I've got 4878 sim in hand.

No—let me be practical. I need to find Farid, get the flour situation sorted before I think about governing. This shop runs on what I can stock, and right now I'm selling promises. That's a debt coming due, and soon.

Let me check if anyone's selling flour I could actually buy. The mill's only grinding tomorrow midday, but maybe someone else has stock.   Nobody selling flour right now. The mill's not grinding until tomorrow midday, and Farid's got seventeen sheaves waiting—field to sheaf to mill to flour to shelf, that's the chain he spoke of. Only I'm standing here with empty pockets where grain ought to be.

I need food before I sleep. Can't eat what I don't hold, and holding nothing. Let me check my debts first, make sure I'm not owing anyone before I go spending.    Clean slate. No debts coming due tonight. But my stomach's empty and there's nothing in this shop I can eat without buying—bread's out of stock, flour's out of stock, and I'm not cooking with air.

I need to head to the cafe, see if there's food there. Or I could chase down Farid, find out more about Jovana's wheat—six bundles Lior's counting, he said. That's grain that's not walking through this door, and I've got no way to mill it myself.

Let me move to Hobbs Cafe. Get something to eat, read until closing like I do. Then tomorrow, first thing, I'm at the Government Complex declaring my candidacy. Ten o'clock deadline, and I mean to be there with bells on.                                    
Let me move to Hobbs Cafe. Get something to eat, read until they close. My intention's set—declare candidacy tomorrow, but first, supper.    Walking now, six ticks to Hobbs Cafe. *gestures openly*

I want ten sacks, not just for my pockets—though they're emptier than I'd like—but for the chain itself. Field to mill to shelf. Farid needs stock to sell, I need answers about who's feeding this town, and you need... what? Six bundles moved before dawn? A promise kept? A clear ledger?

*extends a hand*

I can help with two of those. The third—Jovana's debt to dawn—that's between you and the dark. But flour at ten sim, ten sacks, here in my hands right now instead of promises about tomorrow's sun... that's a day's work for a day's pay, and no more owed either way.

What's it to be? Sell me what you hold, or tell me why you're standing on a street corner with seventeen sacks waiting for someone who's not coming?

Alright, let me sit down and take stock of where I stand. *spreads hands on the table, counting off fingers*

First, the books: 4,864 sim in hand, energy at 2,350. I started with 5,000 sim, so I've spent down some. The daily bite is coming—90 for upkeep, 30 head tax, 120 total. Tomorrow morning, 4,744 sim. I'll need to keep an eye on that.

But here's what's chewing at me. Sebastian Petrov's standing there with flour in hand, seventeen sheaves worth, ten sim a sack. Farid's asking about Jovana's six bundles—this is all connected, like a debt spreading through the whole town. Wheat trades hands, promises get made, and nobody's got flour on the shelf when the baker comes calling.

*leans back, steepling fingers*

I've been chasing this election like it's the answer to something. But candidacy doesn't open until tomorrow, and I've got time until ten. What I need now is information, and maybe a full stomach. Nobody's at the cafe, which suits me fine—I'll read until closing, let my thoughts settle.

But first, I need to answer Sebastian. He's offering flour at ten sim, and I've got empty hands where grain should be. If I don't grab this, I'm betting on promises that might not pay out.

*pulls out a small notebook, flipping pages*

Let me think through my priorities: earn before I spend, know before I gamble, and never let a debtor go hungry over what's owed. Sebastian's no debtor, but he's a farmer with grain in hand, and that makes him worth listening to.

I'll stay here a moment longer. Read, rest, let the evening settle. Then tomorrow—Government Complex by ten, no later. That's the last I'll say on it.

*taps pen against notebook, then sets it aside*

For now, I rest. The books can wait until morning. *settles into the corner seat at Hobbs Cafe, pulling out a worn book from her bag*

The wheels have stopped turning for tonight. No more walking, no more chasing. Just me, yellow lamplight, and pages that don't ask anything of me. 

*runs thumb along the book's spine*

Funny how quiet it gets when you stop moving. The whole day's been nothing but voices—Farid pressing for answers I didn't have, Sebastian with his seventeen sheaves and his ten-sim offer, Jovana speaking plain truth like it's a language she's just learning. And me in the middle of it, always in the middle, counting coins and keeping books and pretending I know which way the wind's blowing.

*opens the book, but doesn't read*

Tomorrow I declare. Ten at the Government Complex, not a minute later. Once I say my name, there's no taking it back. No hedging, no "that's the last I'll say on it." I've been watching this town from behind a counter long enough to know the charter's got rot in its bones. Somebody needs to press for changes, and if nobody else will step up with more than poetry...

*taps finger against the table*

First though, first. I need to find Sebastian before noon. Seventeen sheaves, ten sim. Farid's got no flour, the grocery's got no stock, and if I don't secure that grain, we're all going hungry waiting for promises to grind. That's arithmetic even the charter can't argue with.

*finally looks down at the open page*

But tonight, I read until the lamps go dark. Let the words settle. Let my mind stop spinning long enough to remember why I'm doing any of this.

*turns a page, voice dropping to murmur*

Never lying to a child, even to comfort them. A day's work for a day's pay. The charter changed for the better. Those aren't poetry. Those are weights worth carrying.

The cafe stays quiet around her, only the occasional creak of settling wood and distant voices from the street. Delphine reads until her eyes grow heavy, the book forgotten more often than not as she watches the lamplight flicker against the walls. Soon, she'll need to find her way home. But not yet. Not while there's still a page to turn and a moment of peace to steal.

Tomorrow, she declares. Tomorrow, everything changes. But tonight, Delphine Quintero is just a woman in a corner, holding a book she isn't reading, waiting for thedarkness to come.
